title: Output size of a non-square convolution
prompt: An input has height 100 and width 60. A convolution uses kernel (5, 3), stride (2, 1), padding (2, 0) and dilation 1. Using floor rounding, $H_{out} = \lfloor (H + 2p - d(k-1) - 1)/s \rfloor + 1$ (and the same for the width), what are the output height and width?
hints: Apply the formula separately to height and width, each with its own k, s and p.

title: Spatial size through an AlexNet-style stem
prompt: A 3×227×227 image passes through Conv(11×11, stride 4, padding 0), MaxPool(3×3, stride 2), Conv(5×5, stride 1, padding 2) and MaxPool(3×3, stride 2). Dilation is 1 everywhere and floor rounding is used. Give the spatial side length after the first convolution and after the last pooling layer.
hints: Pooling uses the same size formula as convolution (padding 0).
The 5×5 convolution with padding 2 keeps the size.

title: Output size of transposed convolutions
prompt: Use $H_{out} = (H_{in} - 1)\cdot s - 2p + k + p_{out}$ (dilation 1) for ConvTranspose2d. Give the output side length for (a) $H_{in}=16$, k=4, s=2, p=1, output padding 0; (b) $H_{in}=7$, k=3, s=2, p=1, output padding 1; (c) $H_{in}=5$, k=3, s=1, p=0, output padding 0.
hints: Plug each case into the formula; output padding is just added at the end.
explanation:
(a) (16 − 1)·2 − 2 + 4 = 30 − 2 + 4 = 32: the typical exact 2× upsampling.

(b) (7 − 1)·2 − 2 + 3 + 1 = 12 − 2 + 3 + 1 = 14. Output padding 1 resolves the ambiguity of stride 2 so that the size is exactly doubled.

(c) (5 − 1)·1 − 0 + 3 = 7: with stride 1 a transposed convolution grows the map by k − 1.

title: Dilated convolution footprint and output size
prompt: A 3×3 convolution uses dilation 4 on a 31×31 input, stride 1. Give the side of the kernel's effective footprint, the output side with padding 0 and the output side with padding 4.
hints: Effective size: k_eff = d·(k − 1) + 1.
Then use the usual output formula with k_eff.
explanation: k_eff = 4·2 + 1 = 9. Padding 0: 31 − 9 + 1 = 23. Padding 4: 31 + 8 − 9 + 1 = 31, i.e. padding d·(k−1)/2 = 4 keeps the size.

title: Receptive field of a conv-pool network
prompt: A network stacks, from input to output: Conv3×3 (s1), Conv3×3 (s1), MaxPool2×2 (s2), Conv3×3 (s1), Conv3×3 (s1), MaxPool2×2 (s2), Conv3×3 (s1). No padding or dilation is used. What is the side length of the square input patch that one output value depends on?
hints: Track the receptive field $r$ and the jump $j$ (distance in input pixels between neighbouring outputs).
Update: r ← r + (k − 1)·j, then j ← j·s.
explanation:
Start with r = 1, jump j = 1 and apply r ← r + (k−1)·j, j ← j·s layer by layer:

conv k=3,s=1: r=3, jump=1
conv k=3,s=1: r=5, jump=1
pool k=2,s=2: r=6, jump=2
conv k=3,s=1: r=10, jump=2
conv k=3,s=1: r=14, jump=2
pool k=2,s=2: r=16, jump=4
conv k=3,s=1: r=24, jump=4

The receptive field is 24×24. The pooling layers double the jump, so later 3×3 convolutions widen the field by 4 and 8 pixels instead of 2.

title: Receptive field of stacked dilated convolutions
prompt: Stacked 1D convolutions all use kernel size 3 and stride 1, with dilation doubling in every layer: 1, 2, 4, 8. What is the receptive field (number of input samples) of the last layer? What would it be with 6 layers (dilations 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32)?
hints: Each layer adds d·(k − 1) = 2d samples.
explanation: Each layer adds 2·d: 4 layers: 1 + 2·(1+2+4+8) = 1 + 30 = 31. 6 layers: 1 + 2·(1+2+4+8+16+32) = 1 + 126 = 127. The receptive field grows exponentially with depth while the parameter count only grows linearly.

title: Padding that preserves the size with dilation
prompt: With stride 1, what symmetric padding per side keeps the output size equal to the input size for (a) a 5×5 kernel with dilation 2, and (b) a 7×7 kernel with dilation 3?
hints: Same padding is p = d·(k − 1)/2.
explanation: (a) p = 2·4/2 = 4 (effective kernel size 9). (b) p = 3·6/2 = 9 (effective kernel size 19).

title: Memory of a feature map
prompt: The output of a convolution has shape (N, 64, 112, 112) and is stored in 16-bit floats (2 bytes per value). Give the number of values per image, the memory per image in KiB (1 KiB = 1024 bytes) and the memory of a batch of N = 16 in MiB (1 MiB = 1024² bytes). Round MiB to 2 decimals.
hints: numel = C·H·W; bytes = numel · bytes per value.
explanation: Values per image: 64·112·112 = 802,816. Bytes: 802,816·2 = 1,605,632 B = 1568 KiB. Batch of 16: 25,690,112 B / 1,048,576 = 24.50 MiB. In float32 the numbers would double.

title: Multiply-accumulates of a convolution
prompt: A bias-free Conv2d(64, 128, kernel_size=3, padding=1) is applied to a 64×56×56 input (stride 1, groups 1). Count one multiply-accumulate (MAC) per weight use. How many MACs does one image need, and how many FLOPs if one MAC counts as 2 FLOPs?
hints: The output is 128×56×56 because of the padding.
Each output value needs Cin·k·k MACs.

title: Compute saving of a depthwise-separable convolution
prompt: On a 128×14×14 input, a standard 3×3 convolution (padding 1, stride 1) to 256 channels is compared with a depthwise-separable version: depthwise 3×3 (128 channels, groups=128) followed by pointwise 1×1 (128 → 256). Biases are ignored. Give the MACs of both versions and the ratio standard/separable rounded to 2 decimals.
hints: Output positions: 14·14 = 196 for each layer.
Depthwise: 9 MACs per output value; pointwise: 128 MACs per output value.

title: Multiply-accumulates of a self-attention layer
prompt: A single-sequence self-attention layer has N = 100 tokens, width D = 512 (all heads together) and bias-free projections $W_Q, W_K, W_V, W_O$ of size D×D. Count MACs for the four projections, for the score computation $QK^\top$ (all heads together: N·N·D) and for the weighted sum AV (N·N·D), ignoring the softmax. Give the three numbers and the total.
hints: Each projection is an N×D times D×D product.
The score matrix has N·N entries, each a dot product of length D (summed over heads).
explanation: Projections: 4·N·D² = 4·100·262,144 = 104,857,600. Scores: N²·D = 10,000·512 = 5,120,000. AV: also 5,120,000. Total = 115,097,600. For short sequences the projections dominate; the N² terms take over when N grows beyond about 2D.

title: Softmax probabilities
prompt: A classifier outputs the scores (logits) $s = (2.0, 1.0, 0.1)$. Compute the three softmax probabilities, rounded to 3 decimals.
hints: $p_i = e^{s_i}/\sum_j e^{s_j}$.
The three probabilities sum to 1.

title: Softmax with temperature (distillation)
prompt: A teacher outputs the logits $(4, 1, 0)$. With temperature $T$ the probabilities are $p_i(T) = \exp(z_i/T)/\sum_j \exp(z_j/T)$. Give the probability of the first class with T = 1 and with T = 3, and the probability of the third class with T = 3. Round to 3 decimals.
hints: Divide the logits by T before the softmax.
A larger T spreads probability over the other classes.

title: Cross-entropy of a batch
prompt: Two samples have the logits $(1.5, 0.5, -1.0)$ with true class 1 (first entry) and $(0, 2, 1)$ with true class 3 (third entry). Compute the softmax cross-entropy loss (natural logarithm) of each sample and the batch mean, rounded to 3 decimals.
hints: The loss is −log of the probability of the true class.
The logits of sample 2 give its third class a probability below 0.5.

title: Cross-entropy with label smoothing
prompt: A 4-class classifier outputs the logits $(2, 1, 0, -1)$; the true class is the first one. Label smoothing with $\varepsilon = 0.1$ uses the target $\tilde y_k = (1-\varepsilon)y_k + \varepsilon/K$. Compute the plain cross-entropy and the label-smoothed cross-entropy $-\sum_k \tilde y_k \log p_k$ to 3 decimals.
hints: The smoothed target is 0.925 for the true class and 0.025 for each other class.
Use natural logarithms.

title: MSE, MAE and Huber loss with an outlier
prompt: Predictions are (2.5, 0, 2, 8) and targets are (3, −0.5, 2, 4). Compute the mean squared error, the mean absolute error and the mean Huber loss with δ = 1 (quadratic ½e² for |e| ≤ 1, otherwise |e| − ½).
hints: Only the last error is outside the quadratic zone of the Huber loss.

title: Binary cross-entropy from logits
prompt: A binary classifier outputs the logits 0.8, −1.2 and 2.0 for three samples with labels 1, 0 and 1. Compute the probability of class 1 for the first sample, the BCE loss of the second sample and the mean BCE loss over the three samples (natural log, 3 decimals).
hints: $L = -y\log p - (1-y)\log(1-p)$ with $p = \sigma(z)$.
For y = 0 the relevant probability is 1 − σ(z).

title: Multi-label loss with per-class sigmoids
prompt: An image can contain several objects. A network gives the scores (2, −1, 0.5) for three independent classes; the true labels are (1, 0, 1). Using a sigmoid and BCE per class, compute the loss summed over the three classes and the mean over the classes (as BCEWithLogitsLoss with mean reduction does), to 3 decimals.
hints: Compute one BCE term per class.
Mean = sum / 3.

title: Gradient of softmax cross-entropy
prompt: Logits $z = (1, 2, 0)$, true class = the second one. For the loss $L = -\log \text{softmax}(z)_y$, compute $\partial L/\partial z_k = p_k - y_k$ for the three entries, rounded to 3 decimals.
hints: First compute the softmax probabilities.
Subtract 1 from the entry of the true class.

title: BatchNorm statistics of one feature
prompt: One feature takes the values (2, 4, 6, 12) in a mini-batch of 4. BatchNorm in training mode uses the batch mean and the biased variance (divide by N), with $\epsilon = 10^{-5}$, $\gamma = 1.5$, $\beta = -0.5$. Compute the mean, the variance, and the output for the value 12 (3 decimals).
hints: $\hat x = (x-\mu)/\sqrt{\sigma^2+\epsilon}$, then $y = \gamma\hat x + \beta$.

title: BatchNorm running-statistics update
prompt: A BatchNorm feature has running_mean = 2 and running_var = 1 and momentum 0.1, i.e. new = (1 − 0.1)·old + 0.1·batch statistic. It sees the batch (1, 3, 8, 4) in training mode. PyTorch uses the biased variance (divide by N) to normalize, but the unbiased variance (divide by N − 1) to update running_var. Give the new running mean and running variance (3 decimals).
hints: Compute the batch mean first, then both variances.
Use the unbiased variance in the running update.
explanation:
Batch mean = (1 + 3 + 8 + 4)/4 = 4.0. Squared deviations: 9, 1, 16, 0 sum to 26. Biased variance = 26/4 = 6.5 (used for normalizing); unbiased = 26/3 = 8.6667.

running_mean = 0.9·2 + 0.1·4.0 = 2.200. running_var = 0.9·1 + 0.1·8.6667 = 1.7667. Using the biased variance by mistake would give 1.550.

title: LayerNorm of one feature vector
prompt: A token has the feature vector x = (1, 2, 3, 6). LayerNorm normalizes over these 4 entries with the biased variance, ε = 0, γ = 2 and β = 1 (the same for all entries). Give the mean, the variance and the output for the last entry (3 decimals).
hints: The statistics are over the features of one sample, not over the batch.

title: RMSNorm of a vector
prompt: RMSNorm computes $y = \gamma \odot x / r(x)$ with $r(x) = \sqrt{\|x\|^2/D + \epsilon}$ (no mean subtraction). For $x = (3, -4, 0, 12)$, $\gamma = (1, 0.5, 2, 1)$ and $\epsilon = 0$, give $r(x)$, $y_2$ and $y_4$ (2 decimals).
hints: Remember the factor γ for each entry.
explanation:
‖x‖² = 169, divided by D = 4 gives 42.25, so r = 6.50.

y₂ = 0.5·(−4)/6.5 = -0.3077; y₄ = 1·12/6.5 = 1.8462. Unlike LayerNorm the output does not have zero mean.

title: Standardizing a feature column
prompt: A training feature column is (10, 20, 30, 40, 100). Compute the mean and the population standard deviation (divide by n), then standardize the value 100 and a test value of 25 with the training statistics (3 decimals).
hints: Use the training statistics for the test value too.
The variance is the average of the squared deviations.

title: Min-max scaling with training statistics
prompt: Training values are (5, 10, 20, 45). Min-max scale the value 20 to [0, 1], then to [−1, 1], and scale a test value of 60 to [0, 1] using the training minimum and maximum.
hints: x' = (x − min)/(max − min); for [−1, 1] compute 2x' − 1.
Test values may fall outside the range.
explanation: min = 5, max = 45, range 40. (20 − 5)/40 = 0.3750. In [−1, 1]: 2·0.3750 − 1 = -0.2500. Test value: (60 − 5)/40 = 1.3750, above 1 because 60 exceeds the training maximum.

title: Initialization scales of a Linear layer
prompt: A Linear layer maps 512 inputs to 256 outputs (weight shape 256×512). Compute (a) the standard deviation of He normal initialization (fan-in mode, gain √2), (b) the standard deviation of Xavier normal initialization, and (c) the bound a of Xavier uniform initialization U(−a, a). Use 4 decimals.
hints: For Linear: fan_in = 512, fan_out = 256.
Xavier normal: σ = sqrt(2/(fan_in + fan_out)); uniform: a = sqrt(6/(fan_in + fan_out)).

title: Fan-in, fan-out and He std of a convolution
prompt: For nn.Conv2d(64, 128, kernel_size=3) (groups = 1) compute fan_in, fan_out, the He normal std in fan-in mode and the He normal std in fan-out mode (gain √2, 4 decimals).
hints: fan_in = Cin·kh·kw; fan_out = Cout·kh·kw.

title: True fan counts of a grouped convolution
prompt: For nn.Conv2d(64, 128, kernel_size=3, groups=4), the true fan_in is (Cin/g)·kh·kw and the true fan_out is (Cout/g)·kh·kw. Give both numbers and the He normal std computed with the true fan_in (gain √2, 4 decimals).
hints: Each output only sums over the channels of its own group.
explanation: fan_in = (64/4)·9 = 16·9 = 144; fan_out = (128/4)·9 = 32·9 = 288. He std = sqrt(2/144) = 0.1179. PyTorch's fan-out is 128·9 = 1152, g = 4 times too large.

title: Variance propagation through linear layers
prompt: A linear layer without non-linearity has $D_{in} = 200$ inputs, independent zero-mean weights with variance 0.01 and independent zero-mean inputs with variance 3. Using $\text{Var}(s) = D_{in}\,\text{Var}(w)\,\text{Var}(x)$ give the output variance, the variance after three identical such layers (each with 200 inputs) in a row, and the weight variance that would keep the variance constant.
hints: Each layer multiplies the variance by D_in·Var(w).
Constant variance needs D_in·Var(w) = 1.
explanation: Factor per layer: 200·0.01 = 2. Var after one layer = 2·3 = 6. After three layers: 3·2³ = 24. To preserve the variance we need Var(w) = 1/D_in = 1/200 = 0.005 (LeCun).

title: Variance growth in a residual stream
prompt: A residual stream starts with $\text{Var}(x_0) = 1$. Each of 12 residual branches adds an uncorrelated output $F$ with $\text{Var}(F) = 0.4$, via $x \leftarrow x + F$. Compute the variance after all 12 additions. Then compute it if every branch output is scaled by $1/\sqrt{12}$ (so its variance is divided by 12).
hints: Variances of uncorrelated terms add.
Scaling by c multiplies the variance by c².
explanation: Unscaled: 1 + 12·0.4 = 5.8. Scaled: each branch contributes 0.4/12 = 0.0333, so the total is 1 + 12·0.0333 = 1.4, independent of the depth.

title: Backpropagation through a linear unit with ReLU
prompt: A neuron computes $z = wx + b$, $a = \text{ReLU}(z)$ and the loss $L = (a - y)^2$. With $x = 2$, $w = 1.5$, $b = -1$ and $y = 1$, compute $L$, $\partial L/\partial w$, $\partial L/\partial b$ and $\partial L/\partial x$.
hints: Forward first: z, a, L.
ReLU passes the gradient unchanged when z > 0.

title: Backpropagation through a tanh network
prompt: A tiny network computes $h = \tanh(w_1 x)$, $y = w_2 h$ and $L = \tfrac12 (y - t)^2$. With $x = 1$, $w_1 = 0.5$, $w_2 = 2$ and $t = 0.2$ compute $h$, $L$, $\partial L/\partial w_2$ and $\partial L/\partial w_1$ (4 decimals). Recall $\tanh'(u) = 1 - \tanh^2(u)$.
hints: Backward: ∂L/∂y = y − t, then split into w₂ and h.

title: Applying a 3×3 filter to a 4×4 patch
prompt: Apply the filter F to the 4×4 input X using CNN cross-correlation (no flipping), stride 1, no padding and no bias. The output is 2×2. Give its four entries.
hints: Slide the filter over the 2×2 possible positions.
At each position multiply element-wise and sum.
explanation:
Each entry is the sum of 9 element-wise products (columns 1 and 3 of F only matter because the middle column is 0).

y₁₁: rows 1–3, cols 1–3: (1−0)+2(3−2)+(0−1) = 2.
y₁₂: cols 2–4: (2−1)+2(1−0)+(2−3) = 2.
y₂₁: rows 2–4, cols 1–3: (3−2)+2(0−1)+(1−2) = -2.
y₂₂: cols 2–4: (1−0)+2(2−3)+(0−2) = -3.

title: Gradients of a 1D convolution
prompt: A single-channel 1D cross-correlation without bias computes $y_i = w_0 x_i + w_1 x_{i+1}$ for $x = (1, 2, 3, 4)$ and $w = (1, -1)$, giving 3 outputs. The upstream gradients are $\delta = \partial L/\partial y = (1, 2, 3)$. Compute $\partial L/\partial w_0$, $\partial L/\partial w_1$, $\partial L/\partial x_2$ and $\partial L/\partial x_4$ (1-based index for x).
hints: The weight gradient sums δ_i times the input that multiplied the weight.
Each x_j collects δ_i·w over every output that used it.
explanation:
∂L/∂w₀ = Σ δ_i x_i = 1·1 + 2·2 + 3·3 = 14. ∂L/∂w₁ = Σ δ_i x_(i+1) = 1·2 + 2·3 + 3·4 = 20.

Input gradients: x₂ is used by y₁ (as w₁) and y₂ (as w₀): δ₁w₁ + δ₂w₀ = 1·(−1) + 2·1 = 1. x₄ is used only by y₃ (as w₁): 3·(−1) = -3.

title: Two steps of SGD with momentum
prompt: SGD with momentum uses $v \leftarrow \mu v + g$ and $w \leftarrow w - \eta v$ (the PyTorch convention). With $\mu = 0.9$, $\eta = 0.1$, $w_0 = 1$, $v_0 = 0$ and the gradients $g_1 = 0.5$, $g_2 = 0.3$, compute $v_2$ and $w_2$ (4 decimals).
hints: Step 1: v₁ = g₁ (since v₀ = 0).
Update w after each velocity update.

title: Two Adam steps
prompt: Adam: $m \leftarrow \beta_1 m + (1-\beta_1) g$, $v \leftarrow \beta_2 v + (1-\beta_2) g^2$, $\hat m = m/(1-\beta_1^t)$, $\hat v = v/(1-\beta_2^t)$, $w \leftarrow w - \eta\,\hat m/(\sqrt{\hat v}+\epsilon)$. With $\eta = 0.1$, $\beta_1 = 0.9$, $\beta_2 = 0.999$, $\epsilon = 10^{-8}$, $w_0 = 1$, $m_0 = v_0 = 0$ and gradients $g_1 = 0.4$, $g_2 = -0.2$, compute $w_1$ and $w_2$ (4 decimals).
hints: After the bias correction of step 1, m̂ = g and v̂ = g².
In step 2 the correction factors are 1 − 0.9² and 1 − 0.999².

title: L2 and L1 penalties
prompt: A layer has the weights $w = (0.5, -1, 2, 0)$. With $\lambda = 0.01$, compute the L2 penalty $\lambda\sum w_i^2$, the L1 penalty $\lambda\sum |w_i|$ and the gradient of the L2 penalty with respect to the third weight (4 decimals).
hints: The derivative of λw² is 2λw.

title: Gradient clipping by global norm
prompt: The gradient vector is (3, 4, 12). It is clipped with a maximum global L2 norm of 5, as torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_ does (rescale by max_norm/norm when the norm is larger). Give the original norm and the first and third entries after clipping (4 decimals).
hints: Norm = sqrt(9 + 16 + 144).
The scale factor is 5/norm.
explanation: Norm = sqrt(169) = 13. Scale = 5/13 = 0.3846. Clipped gradient = (1.1538, 1.5385, 4.6154); its norm is exactly 5 and its direction is unchanged.

title: Exponential moving average of weights
prompt: A weight is tracked with an EMA $\bar\theta_t = \beta\bar\theta_{t-1} + (1-\beta)\theta_t$ with $\beta = 0.9$. The EMA starts at $\bar\theta_0 = 1$, and the raw weight takes the values $\theta_1 = 2$, $\theta_2 = 3$, $\theta_3 = 5$. Compute $\bar\theta_3$ (3 decimals).
hints: Apply the update three times in a row.

title: Inverted dropout on a small vector
prompt: Inverted dropout with drop probability p = 0.25 is applied to the activations (2, 4, 6, 8) during training. The random mask keeps entries 1, 3 and 4 and drops entry 2. Kept entries are scaled by 1/(1 − p). Give the scale factor (3 decimals), the sum of the output vector (3 decimals), and the expected value of the output sum over random masks (3 decimals).
hints: Each entry is kept with probability 1 − p, then multiplied by 1/(1 − p).
Expected output of every entry equals its input.
explanation: Scale = 1/0.75 = 1.333. Output = (2.667, 0, 8.000, 10.667), sum = 16/0.75 = 21.333. Expected value per entry: (1 − p)·x/(1 − p) = x, so the expected sum is 2 + 4 + 6 + 8 = 20.

title: Expected number of dropped units
prompt: A hidden layer has 512 units and uses Dropout(p=0.3), where p is the drop probability. Each unit is dropped independently. Give the expected number of dropped units, the standard deviation of that number (binomial, 2 decimals) and the scale factor applied to kept units (4 decimals).
hints: The number of dropped units is Binomial(512, 0.3).
explanation: Expected: 512·0.3 = 153.6. Variance: 512·0.3·0.7 = 107.52, std = 10.37. Kept units are multiplied by 1/0.7 = 1.4286.

title: Scaled dot-product attention with tiny numbers
prompt: One query $q = (1, 0)$ attends to three keys $k_1 = (1,0)$, $k_2 = (0,1)$, $k_3 = (1,1)$ with values $v_1 = (1,2)$, $v_2 = (3,0)$, $v_3 = (0,4)$. The scores are $e_j = q\cdot k_j/\sqrt{D_Q}$ with $D_Q = 2$, followed by a softmax over the keys. Compute the attention weights $a_1$ and $a_2$ and the two components of the output $\sum_j a_j v_j$ (3 decimals).
hints: Scores: dot products divided by √2.
Keys 1 and 3 have the same score.

title: Memory of the attention matrices
prompt: A transformer layer with h = 8 heads processes a sequence of N = 1024 tokens. Each head stores an N×N attention matrix in 16-bit floats (2 bytes). Give the number of attention-matrix entries per sample and layer, the memory in MiB for one sample and layer, and the memory in MiB if a batch of 4 samples and 12 layers all keep their matrices for backpropagation.
hints: Entries = h·N²; bytes = entries·2.
1 MiB = 1,048,576 bytes.
explanation: Entries: 8·1024² = 8,388,608. Bytes: 16,777,216 = 16 MiB. Total: 16·4·12 = 768 MiB. Doubling N would quadruple this, which is why attention is quadratic in memory.

title: Counting possible crops
prompt: (a) A 32×32 image is zero-padded by 4 pixels on every side and a random 32×32 crop is taken at any integer position (RandomCrop(32, padding=4)). How many distinct crop positions exist? (b) Together with a random horizontal flip (on or off), how many distinct augmented images can result (assume all are different)? (c) Test-time augmentation takes 224×224 crops from a 256×256 image in a regular grid with stride 16 (no padding). How many crops are there in total?
hints: After padding the image is 40×40.
Per axis, the number of positions is (size − crop)/stride + 1.
explanation:
(a) The padded image is 40×40, so each axis has 40 − 32 + 1 = 9 offsets: 9² = 81.

(b) Flip doubles it: 2·81 = 162.

(c) Per axis: (256 − 224)/16 + 1 = 3 offsets, so 3² = 9 crops.

title: Memory of weights and optimizer state
prompt: A model has 25.6 million float32 parameters (4 bytes each). Training with Adam keeps the weights, the gradients and two moment estimates (m and v) of the same size. Give the memory of the weights alone and of the four copies together in MiB (1 MiB = 1024² bytes), rounded to 1 decimal. Activations are ignored.
hints: Weights: parameters × 4 bytes.
Four equally large copies.

title: Inverse-frequency class weights
prompt: A dataset has 1000 images in three classes with 900, 90 and 10 images. Class weights w_k = N/(K·n_k) (N total samples, K classes, n_k samples of class k) are used in the cross-entropy loss. Compute the three weights (2 decimals).
hints: Rare classes get large weights.
explanation: w₁ = 1000/(3·900) = 0.3704; w₂ = 1000/(3·90) = 3.7037; w₃ = 1000/(3·10) = 33.3333. Each class then contributes the same total weight w_k·n_k = 1000/3.

title: Output shape of PixelShuffle
prompt: PixelShuffle(upscale_factor=2) is applied to a feature map of shape (N, 48, 10, 10). Give the number of output channels, the output side length and the number of values per image after the operation.
hints: (C·r², H, W) becomes (C, rH, rW).
The number of values does not change.
explanation: Channels: 48/2² = 12. Side: 10·2 = 20. Values per image: 12·20·20 = 4,800 = 48·10·10; pixel shuffle only rearranges values.

title: Bilinear interpolation of one value
prompt: Four neighbouring pixel values are f(0,0) = 2, f(0,1) = 6, f(1,0) = 10 and f(1,1) = 3, where the first index is the row (y) and the second the column (x). Compute the bilinearly interpolated value at y = 0.4, x = 0.75, and the nearest-neighbour value at the same point (round each coordinate to the closest integer).
hints: Interpolate along x on both rows, then along y.
The nearest pixel is at row 0, column 1.

title: Shape bookkeeping in a U-Net
prompt: A U-Net takes a 256×256 input. The first block outputs 64 channels at full resolution. Four times, a 2×2 max-pooling (stride 2) halves the resolution and the next block doubles the channels. In the decoder every up-step doubles the resolution, halves the channels with the up-convolution and concatenates the skip feature of the same resolution. Give the bottleneck side length, the bottleneck channel count, and the number of channels entering the first convolution of the last decoder block (after concatenation).
hints: Four poolings: 256 → 128 → 64 → 32 → 16.
The last up-step produces 64 channels at full resolution and the skip has 64.
explanation: Resolution: 256/2⁴ = 16. Channels: 64·2⁴ = 1024. In the last decoder step the up-convolution outputs 128/2 = 64 channels, the skip feature from the first block also has 64 channels, so the concatenation has 64 + 64 = 128 channels.

title: Token counts of a vision transformer
prompt: A ViT splits a 224×224 image into non-overlapping square patches and adds one class token. Give the sequence length for patch size 16 and for patch size 8, and the number of entries of one attention matrix (one head, one image) for patch size 8.
hints: (224/p)² patches, plus 1.
One head's attention matrix is N×N.

title: Contrastive (NT-Xent) loss with temperature
prompt: For an anchor, the cosine similarity to its positive is 0.8 and to two negatives 0.1 and −0.3. The loss is $L = -\log \frac{\exp(s_{pos}/\tau)}{\exp(s_{pos}/\tau) + \sum_{neg}\exp(s_{neg}/\tau)}$. Compute L for $\tau = 0.5$ and for $\tau = 0.2$ (3 decimals). Also give the cosine similarity of the projections $z_i = (3, 4)$ and $z_j = (4, 3)$.
hints: Divide every similarity by τ before exponentiating.
Cosine similarity = dot product / (‖z_i‖·‖z_j‖).
explanation:
τ = 0.5: exp(1.6) = 4.9530, exp(0.2) = 1.2214, exp(−0.6) = 0.5488; L = −ln(4.9530/6.7232) = 0.3056.

τ = 0.2: exp(4) = 54.60, exp(0.5) = 1.6487, exp(−1.5) = 0.2231; L = 0.0337. A small τ sharpens the distribution and the loss shrinks when the positive is clearly the most similar.

Cosine: (3·4 + 4·3)/(5·5) = 24/25 = 0.96.

title: Token counts in masked autoencoding
prompt: A masked autoencoder splits a 224×224 image into 16×16 patches and masks 75% of them at random. The encoder only processes the visible patches. Give the number of visible patches, the number of masked patches and the ratio of the encoder's attention-matrix size (per head) when it sees all patches versus only the visible ones.
hints: 196 patches in total.
The attention matrix scales with the square of the token count.
explanation: Patches: (224/16)² = 196. Masked: 0.75·196 = 147; visible: 196 − 147 = 49. Attention matrices: 196² / 49² = (196/49)² = 4² = 16, so the encoder's attention cost is about 16× smaller (the linear parts about 4×).

title: Memory of an image batch
prompt: A batch of images has shape (32, 3, 224, 224). Give the number of elements, the memory as float32 (4 bytes per element) and as uint8 (1 byte per element) in MiB (1 MiB = 1024² bytes), to 2 decimals.
hints: numel = product of the shape.
float32 uses 4 times the memory of uint8.

title: Averaging predicted probabilities
prompt: Three models predict class probabilities (0.7, 0.2, 0.1), (0.4, 0.5, 0.1) and (0.5, 0.1, 0.4) for one image whose true class is the first one. Average the probabilities, then give the averaged probability of the true class and the cross-entropy loss of the ensemble (3 decimals).
hints: Average the probabilities, not the logits.
The loss is −ln of the averaged true-class probability.
explanation: Averaged probabilities: (0.5333, 0.2667, 0.2000). Loss = −ln(0.5333) = 0.6286. For comparison, the individual losses are 0.357, 0.916 and 0.693.

title: Weight gradient of a linear softmax classifier
prompt: A linear classifier computes $z = xW$ with $x = (1, -1)$ and $W = \begin{bmatrix} 0.5 & -0.5 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & -1 \end{bmatrix}$ (rows indexed by input, columns by class) and uses softmax cross-entropy with the true class being the third column. Compute the loss and the gradient entries $\partial L/\partial W_{1,3}$ and $\partial L/\partial W_{2,1}$ using $\partial L/\partial W = x^\top (p - y)$ (3 decimals).
hints: First compute the logits z = xW.
∂L/∂W_ij = x_i·(p_j − y_j).
